Where to Read / Novel

Subject

Novel

Longer fiction still in the public domain: social worlds, moral arguments, and plots that have outlasted their first printers. Each card below is a catalog entry, not a file stored here.

Pride and Prejudice

Pride and Prejudice

by Jane Austen

Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy misjudge each other in a comedy of marriage, income, and pride. Austen’s second published novel is still the surest entrance to her shelf.

Emma

Emma

by Jane Austen

Emma Woodhouse has money, leisure, and a talent for arranging other people’s lives. The novel lets her be charming and wrong in the same sentence.

Sense and Sensibility

Sense and Sensibility

by Jane Austen

Two sisters, turned out of their home, try sense and feeling as ways of surviving love and reduced means. It was Austen’s first published novel.

Persuasion

Persuasion

by Jane Austen

Anne Elliot broke an engagement years ago and has had to live quietly with the decision. A return of the man she refused gives the book its second chance.

Jane Eyre

Jane Eyre

by Charlotte Brontë

An orphan becomes a governess and refuses every arrangement that would make her less than a person. The house at Thornfield holds a secret the marriage plot cannot step around.

Wuthering Heights

Wuthering Heights

by Emily Brontë

Heathcliff and Catherine’s attachment wrecks two households across two generations. The story is told by a tenant and a housekeeper, never by the pair at its center.

Frankenstein

Frankenstein

by Mary Shelley

Victor Frankenstein builds a living being and then abandons it. The creature’s education, and Victor’s refusal to answer for what he made, are the book’s real experiment.

Dracula

Dracula

by Bram Stoker

Jonathan Harker’s travel diary opens onto a count who intends to move to London. The rest of the novel is a coalition of notes, blood, and timetables trying to stop him.

The Picture of Dorian Gray

The Picture of Dorian Gray

by Oscar Wilde

A young man wishes that a portrait would age in his place. Wilde’s only novel follows the wish into influence, cruelty, and a picture locked in a room.

The Hound of the Baskervilles

The Hound of the Baskervilles

by Arthur Conan Doyle

A family legend about a hound on the Devon moor brings Holmes out of a silence Doyle had meant to be permanent. The rational explanation has to earn its place against the fog.

Treasure Island

Treasure Island

by Robert Louis Stevenson

Jim Hawkins finds a map and goes to sea with a crew that is not what the advertisement promised. Long John Silver remains the model of a charming villain.

The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde

The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde

by Robert Louis Stevenson

A London lawyer tries to understand the tie between a respectable doctor and a violent man who shares his house. Stevenson’s short novel is a study of a self split on purpose.

A Tale of Two Cities

A Tale of Two Cities

by Charles Dickens

London and Paris before and during the French Revolution, joined by a look-alike, a prisoner, and a sacrifice. The opening sentence is famous; the plot earns it.

Great Expectations

Great Expectations

by Charles Dickens

Pip is lifted out of a forge by money whose source he misunderstands. Dickens’s late novel is about class, gratitude, and the patron Pip invents in his head.

Moby-Dick

Moby-Dick

by Herman Melville

Ishmael ships on the Pequod under a captain hunting one white whale. The book stops for whales, work, and metaphysics, then returns to the chase.

Adventures of Huckleberry Finn

Adventures of Huckleberry Finn

by Mark Twain

Huck Finn fakes his death and rafts the Mississippi with Jim, who is escaping enslavement. Twain’s novel is funny, and it does not let the joke forgive the country it travels.

Little Women

Little Women

by Louisa May Alcott

Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy March grow up in a household short of money and long on opinions. Jo’s wish to write is as much the plot as any marriage.

Anne of Green Gables

Anne of Green Gables

by L. M. Montgomery

Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert ask for a boy from the orphanage and receive Anne Shirley. She talks, imagines, and slowly makes herself necessary to Avonlea.

The Secret Garden

The Secret Garden

by Frances Hodgson Burnett

Mary Lennox arrives at a Yorkshire manor and finds a garden no one is allowed to enter. Tending it changes her, and the cousin shut in another room.

The Call of the Wild

The Call of the Wild

by Jack London

Buck, a stolen California dog, is worked north into the Yukon. London tells the story from the animal’s side of the harness.

The Time Machine

The Time Machine

by H. G. Wells

A Victorian inventor rides his machine to a future in which humanity has split. Wells’s novella is a social argument dressed as a traveler’s report.

The War of the Worlds

The War of the Worlds

by H. G. Wells

Martian cylinders fall on the English countryside and the narrator walks through the collapse of ordinary life. Wells aimed the invasion at the empire that had invaded others.

The Awakening

The Awakening

by Kate Chopin

Edna Pontellier, a wife in Creole New Orleans, stops agreeing that her life is already decided. Chopin’s novel was received coldly and later read as a classic.

Crime and Punishment

Crime and Punishment

by Fyodor Dostoevsky

Raskolnikov tests a theory that some people may kill for a higher purpose, and the theory does not survive the act. This entry points to a public-domain English translation.

Anna Karenina

Anna Karenina

by Leo Tolstoy

Anna’s affair and Levin’s search for a workable life run side by side in imperial Russia. Tolstoy gives the social world as much weight as the passion. The link is to a public-domain English translation.

The Count of Monte Cristo

The Count of Monte Cristo

by Alexandre Dumas

Edmond Dantès is imprisoned on a false charge and comes back, years later, with a new name and a plan. Dumas makes patience itself into an adventure.

Les Misérables

Les Misérables

by Victor Hugo

Jean Valjean leaves prison and is pursued across France by Inspector Javert, while Hugo pauses to write about sewers, convents, and justice. The catalog links a public-domain English translation.

Don Quixote

Don Quixote

by Miguel de Cervantes

A country gentleman renames himself a knight and rides out to enforce the plots of chivalric books. Cervantes’s novel is the comedy of taking reading literally. The link is to a public-domain English translation.

The Scarlet Letter

The Scarlet Letter

by Nathaniel Hawthorne

Hester Prynne wears a letter the town requires, while the father of her child stays unnamed. Hawthorne’s novel is about punishment as a public art.

The Great Gatsby

The Great Gatsby

by F. Scott Fitzgerald

Nick Carraway rents a house next to Jay Gatsby’s parties and slowly learns what the parties are for.

Through the Looking-Glass

Through the Looking-Glass

by Lewis Carroll

Through the Looking-Glass is the sequel to his Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, in which many of the characters were anthropomorphic playing cards. In this second novel the theme is chess.

Moby-Dick; or, The Whale

Moby-Dick; or, The Whale

by Herman Melville

Moby-Dick; or, The Whale turns on the sailor Ishmael's narrative of the maniacal quest of Ahab, captain of the whaling ship Pequod, for vengeance against Moby Dick, the giant white sperm whale that bit off his leg on the ship's previous voyage.

The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Complete

The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Complete

by Mark Twain

The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Complete is set in the 1830s–1840s in the fictional town of St. Petersburg, which is based on Hannibal, Missouri, where Twain lived as a boy. In the novel, Sawyer has several adventures, often with his friend Huckleberry Finn.

The House of the Seven Gables

The House of the Seven Gables

by Nathaniel Hawthorne

The House of the Seven Gables stays with a New England family and their ancestral home. In the book, Hawthorne explores themes of guilt, retribution, and atonement, and colors the tale with suggestions of the supernatural and witchcraft.

Ivanhoe: A Romance

Ivanhoe: A Romance

by Walter Scott

In Ivanhoe: A Romance, the Waverley novels are considered seminal to the genre of historical fiction, and Ivanhoe became by far the best-known entry in the whole cycle of nearly thirty books. Ivanhoe marked a shift away from Scott's prior practice of setting stories in Scotland during centuries closer to the one from which he wrote his books.

Tom Sawyer Abroad

Tom Sawyer Abroad

by Mark Twain

Tom Sawyer Abroad features Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn in a parody of adventure stories like those of Jules Verne.

Tom Sawyer, Detective

Tom Sawyer, Detective

by Mark Twain

Tom Sawyer, Detective is a sequel to The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, and Tom Sawyer Abroad. Tom Sawyer attempts to solve a mysterious murder in this burlesque of the immensely popular detective novels of the time.

The Tragedy of Pudd'nhead Wilson

The Tragedy of Pudd'nhead Wilson

by Mark Twain

In The Tragedy of Pudd'nhead Wilson, the central intrigue revolves around two boys—one, born into slavery, with 1/32 black ancestry; the other, white, born to be the master of the house. The two boys, who look similar, are switched at infancy.

Far from the Madding Crowd

Far from the Madding Crowd

by Thomas Hardy

Far from the Madding Crowd originally appeared anonymously as a monthly serial in Cornhill Magazine, where it gained a wide readership. Far from the Madding Crowd is set in Thomas Hardy's Wessex in rural southwest England, as had been his earlier Under the Greenwood Tree.

Tess of the d'Urbervilles: A Pure Woman

Tess of the d'Urbervilles: A Pure Woman

by Thomas Hardy

Tess of the d'Urbervilles: A Pure Woman initially appeared in a censored and serialised version, published by the British illustrated newspaper The Graphic, then in book form in three volumes, and as a single volume. Although now considered a major novel of the 19th century, Tess of the d'Urbervilles received mixed reviews when it first appeared, in part because it challenged the morals of late Victorian England.

Freckles

Freckles

by Gene Stratton-Porter

Freckles is primarily set in the Limberlost Swamp area of Indiana, with brief scenes set in Chicago. The title character also appears briefly in Porter's A Girl of the Limberlost.

A Tramp Abroad

A Tramp Abroad

by Mark Twain

A Tramp Abroad details a journey by the author, with his friend Harris (a character created for the book, and based on his closest friend, Joseph Twichell), through central and southern Europe. While the stated goal of the journey is to walk most of the way, the men find themselves using other forms of transport as they traverse the continent.

The Return of the Native

The Return of the Native

by Thomas Hardy

The Return of the Native first appeared in the magazine Belgravia, a publication known for its sensationalism, and was presented in 12 monthly instalments from 9 January to 19 December. Because of the novel's controversial themes, Hardy had some difficulty finding a publisher; reviews, however, though somewhat mixed, were generally positive.

The Pilgrim's Progress from this world to that which is to come Delivered under the similitude of a dream, by John Bunyan

The Pilgrim's Progress from this world to that which is to come Delivered under the similitude of a dream, by John Bunyan

by John Bunyan

In The Pilgrim's Progress from this world to that which is to come Delivered under the similitude of a dream, by John Bunyan, the Pilgrim's Progress from This World, to That Which Is to Come is a Christian allegory written by the English nonconformist preacher John Bunyan.

The Damnation of Theron Ware

The Damnation of Theron Ware

by Harold Frederic

In The Damnation of Theron Ware, Set in the fictional town of Octavius in upstate New York, the novel presents a portrait of late 19th-century provincial United States, the religious life of its ethnic groups, and its intellectual and artistic culture. According to Publishers Weekly, it was the fifth-best-selling book in the United States.

Maria; Or, The Wrongs of Woman

Maria; Or, The Wrongs of Woman

by Mary Wollstonecraft

In Maria; Or, The Wrongs of Woman, Maria: or, The Wrongs of Woman is Mary Wollstonecraft's unfinished novelistic sequel to her revolutionary political treatise A Vindication of the Rights of Woman. The Wrongs of Woman was published posthumously in by her husband, William Godwin, and is often considered her most radical feminist work.

Mansfield Park

Mansfield Park

by Jane Austen

In Mansfield Park, a second edition was published in by John Murray, still within Austen's lifetime. Mansfield Park did not receive any public reviews until.

The Mayor of Casterbridge

The Mayor of Casterbridge

by Thomas Hardy

In The Mayor of Casterbridge, one of Hardy's Wessex novels, it is set in a fictional rural England with Casterbridge standing in for Dorchester in Dorset where the author spent his youth. The Mayor of Casterbridge was first published as a weekly serialisation from January.

A Little Princess Being the whole story of Sara Crewe now told for the first time

A Little Princess Being the whole story of Sara Crewe now told for the first time

by Frances Hodgson Burnett

In A Little Princess Being the whole story of Sara Crewe now told for the first time, All three versions tell the story of Sara Crewe, a wealthy young girl and the prize student of a private London boarding school who is reduced to poverty and forced to endure the life of a servant under the school's cruel headmistress.

Jude the Obscure

Jude the Obscure

by Thomas Hardy

In Jude the Obscure, the protagonist, Jude Fawley, is a working-class young man; he is a stonemason who dreams of becoming a scholar. The other main character is his cousin, Sue Bridehead, who is also his central love interest.

The Rise of Silas Lapham

The Rise of Silas Lapham

by William Dean Howells

The Rise of Silas Lapham stays with the materialistic rise of Silas Lapham from rags to riches, and his ensuing moral susceptibility. Silas earns a fortune in the paint business, but he lacks social standards, which he tries to attain through his daughter's marriage into the aristocratic Corey family.

The Moonstone

The Moonstone

by Wilkie Collins

The Moonstone is an early example of the modern detective novel, and established many of the ground rules of the modern genre. Its publication was started on 4 January 1868 and was completed on 8 August 1868.

Daddy-Long-Legs

Daddy-Long-Legs

by Jean Webster

Daddy-Long-Legs stays with the protagonist, Jerusha "Judy" Abbott, as she leaves an orphanage and is sent to college by a benefactor whom she has never seen. Daddy-Long-Legs was initially serialized in the April–September issues of the Ladies' Home Journal, and first published in book form by The Century Company on September 28,.

McTeague: A Story of San Francisco

McTeague: A Story of San Francisco

by Frank Norris

McTeague: A Story of San Francisco recounts a couple's courtship and marriage, and their subsequent descent into poverty and violence as the result of jealousy and greed. McTeague: A Story of San Francisco was the basis for the films McTeague and Erich von Stroheim's Greed.

Charlotte Temple

Charlotte Temple

by Mrs. Rowson

Charlotte Temple recounts a schoolgirl, Charlotte Temple, who is seduced by a British officer and brought to America, where she is abandoned, pregnant, sick and in poverty. The first American edition was published in 1794 and the novel became a bestseller.

The Phantom of the Opera

The Phantom of the Opera

by Gaston Leroux

The Phantom of the Opera was first published as a serial in Le Gaulois from 23 September to 8 January, and was released in volume form in late March by Pierre Lafitte. The Phantom of the Opera is partly inspired by historical events at the Paris Opera during the nineteenth century, and by an apocryphal tale concerning the use of a former ballet pupil's skeleton in a production of Carl Maria von Weber's Der Freischütz.

The American

The American

by Henry James

The American is an uneasy combination of social comedy and melodrama concerning the adventures and misadventures of Christopher Newman, an essentially good-hearted but rather gauche American businessman on his first tour of Europe.

The Europeans

The Europeans

by Henry James

The Europeans is a comedy contrasting the behaviour and attitudes of two visitors from Europe with those of their relatives living in the "New" World of New England. The Europeans first appeared as a serial in The Atlantic Monthly for July–October.

Uncle Tom's Cabin

Uncle Tom's Cabin

by Harriet Beecher Stowe

In Uncle Tom's Cabin, Published in two volumes, the novel had a profound effect on attitudes toward African Americans and slavery in the U. and is said to have "helped lay the groundwork for the American Civil War".

Daisy Miller: A Study

Daisy Miller: A Study

by Henry James

In Daisy Miller: A Study, Daisy Miller, A Study is a novella by Henry James that first appeared in The Cornhill Magazine in June–July, and in book form the following year. Daisy Miller: A Study portrays the courtship of the beautiful American girl Daisy Miller by Winterbourne, a sophisticated compatriot of hers.

The Aspern Papers

The Aspern Papers

by Henry James

One of James's best-known and most acclaimed longer tales, The Aspern Papers is based on the letters Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote to Mary Shelley's stepsister, Claire Clairmont, who saved them until she died. Set in Venice, The Aspern Papers demonstrates James's ability to generate suspense while never neglecting the development of his characters.

A pair of blue eyes

A pair of blue eyes

by Thomas Hardy

A pair of blue eyes was the first of Hardy's novels to bear his name and was included by Hardy in his "romances and fantasies".

The Octopus : A Story of California

The Octopus : A Story of California

by Frank Norris

The Octopus: A Story of California describes the wheat industry in California, and the conflicts between wheat growers and a railway company. Norris was inspired to write the novel by the Mussel Slough Tragedy involving the Southern Pacific Railroad.

Black Beauty

Black Beauty

by Anna Sewell

Black Beauty was written from a horse as main character's perspective. She wrote it in the last years of her life, during which she was bedridden and seriously ill.

Laddie: A True Blue Story

Laddie: A True Blue Story

by Gene Stratton-Porter

In Laddie: A True Blue Story, Laddie is an American silent drama film directed by James Leo Meehan with John Bowers in the title role. Laddie: A True Blue Story was based on Gene Stratton-Porter's novel, Laddie, A True Blue Story (1913).

The Cash Boy

The Cash Boy

by Horatio, Jr. Alger

Adoptees, orphans, Baseball, and adventure stories, in Horatio, Jr. Alger’s Cash Boy.

The Count's Millions

The Count's Millions

by Emile Gaboriau

Detective and mystery stories, in Emile Gaboriau’s Count's Millions.

Three men in a boat (to say nothing of the dog)

Three men in a boat (to say nothing of the dog)

by Jerome K. (Jerome Klapka) Jerome

In Three men in a boat (to say nothing of the dog), Jerome describing a two-week boating holiday on the Thames from Kingston upon Thames to Oxford and back to Kingston. Three men in a boat (to say nothing of the dog) was initially intended to be a serious travel guide, with accounts of local history along the route, but the humorous elements took over to the point where the serious and somewhat sentimental passages seem a distraction from the comic novel.

Moran of the Lady Letty

Moran of the Lady Letty

by Frank Norris

In Moran of the Lady Letty, Melford and Valentino had previously worked together on the box office hit The Sheik,. The film is based on the novel of the same name by Frank Norris and was adapted for the screen by Monte Katterjohn.

A Knight of the Cumberland

A Knight of the Cumberland

by John, Jr. Fox

In A Knight of the Cumberland, the writing of John Fox, Jr. has had profound significance in the way America studies turn-of-the-century Appalachian mountain life, lending fondness for its customs, respect for its survival, and deep regard for its environmental and psychological altercations.

A Dream of John Ball; and, A King's Lesson

A Dream of John Ball; and, A King's Lesson

by William Morris

A Dream of John Ball; and, A King's Lesson features the rebel priest John Ball, who was accused of being a Lollard. He is famed for his question "When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?

Miss Billy — Married

Miss Billy — Married

by Eleanor H. (Eleanor Hodgman) Porter

Married women and marriage, in Eleanor H. (Eleanor Hodgman) Porter’s Miss Billy — Married.

The Country of the Pointed Firs

The Country of the Pointed Firs

by Sarah Orne Jewett

The Country of the Pointed Firs is considered by some literary critics to be her finest work.

The Fortunes and Misfortunes of the Famous Moll Flanders

The Fortunes and Misfortunes of the Famous Moll Flanders

by Daniel Defoe

The Fortunes and Misfortunes of the Famous Moll Flanders purports to be an autobiographical account of the life of the eponymous heroine, detailing her exploits from birth until old age as she uses her wits, cunning and charm to provide herself with financial security. While the novel is now generally attributed to Defoe, and his name is given as the author in modern printings, the original text does not list an author and was presented as an autobiography.

A Journal of the Plague Year Being Observations or Memorials of the Most Remarkable Occurrences, as Well Public as Private, Which Happened in London During the Last Great Visitation in 1665. Written by a Citizen Who Continued All the While in London

A Journal of the Plague Year Being Observations or Memorials of the Most Remarkable Occurrences, as Well Public as Private, Which Happened in London During the Last Great Visitation in 1665. Written by a Citizen Who Continued All the While in London

by Daniel Defoe

A Journal of the Plague Year Being Observations or Memorials of the Most Remarkable Occurrences, as Well Public as Private, Which is an account of one man's experiences of the year, in which the bubonic plague struck the city of London in what became known as the Great Plague of London, the last epidemic of plague in that city, as part of the larger, centuries-long second plague pandemic.

The Holy War, Made by King Shaddai Upon Diabolus, for the Regaining of the Metropolis of the World; Or, The Losing and Taking Again of the Town of Mansoul

The Holy War, Made by King Shaddai Upon Diabolus, for the Regaining of the Metropolis of the World; Or, The Losing and Taking Again of the Town of Mansoul

by John Bunyan

In The Holy War, Made by King Shaddai Upon Diabolus, for the Regaining of the Metropolis of the World; Or, The Losing and Taking Again of, Regarded as one of the early modern English novel written in the form of an allegory, it recounts the residents in a town called "Mansoul" (Man's soul). Though the town along with its citizens is deemed perfect under the rule of Shaddai (Almighty), its citizens had been persuaded by Diabolus to rebel and throw off his reign, effectively crowning Diabolus as its ruler.

The King's Jackal

The King's Jackal

by Richard Harding Davis

Kings and rulers, in Richard Harding Davis’ King's Jackal.

The Romany Rye

The Romany Rye

by George Borrow

The Romany Rye is a novel by George Borrow, written in as a sequel to Lavengro.

The Grain of Dust: A Novel

The Grain of Dust: A Novel

by David Graham Phillips

Love stories and Man-woman relationships, in David Graham Phillips’ Grain of Dust: A Novel.

The Fortune Hunter

The Fortune Hunter

by David Graham Phillips

Man-woman relationships, in David Graham Phillips’ Fortune Hunter.

The Ambassadors

The Ambassadors

by Henry James

The Ambassadors is a dark comedy which follows the trip of protagonist Lewis Lambert Strether to Paris, France to bring Chad Newsome, the son of his widowed fiancée, Mrs Newsome, back to the family business. The Ambassadors is written in the third-person, from Strether's point of view.

The Conflict

The Conflict

by David Graham Phillips

Man-woman relationships, social classes in United States, and women in social conditions, in David Graham Phillips’ Conflict.

Just David

Just David

by Eleanor H. (Eleanor Hodgman) Porter

Just David was among the top six bestsellers in cities across the United States, and in July it was the second bestselling novel. Originally published by Houghton Mifflin, it recounts a young boy, David, who must learn to adapt to living with others after the death of his reclusive father; along the way, the villagers and his adoptive parents adapt as much or more to him.

Maggie: A Girl of the Streets

Maggie: A Girl of the Streets

by Stephen Crane

Maggie: A Girl of the Streets turns on Margaret "Maggie" Johnson, an 18-year-old girl from the Bowery who is driven to prostitution due to her failed relationship with a young man named Pete Murphy who leaves her for another girl named Nellie Griffiths, and also due to poverty and solitude.

Susan Lenox: Her Fall and Rise

Susan Lenox: Her Fall and Rise

by David Graham Phillips

In Susan Lenox: Her Fall and Rise, Leonard and starring Greta Garbo and Clark Gable. The film is based on a novel by David Graham Phillips.

The Price She Paid

The Price She Paid

by David Graham Phillips

Man-woman relationships, in David Graham Phillips’ Price She Paid.

The Errand Boy; Or, How Phil Brent Won Success

The Errand Boy; Or, How Phil Brent Won Success

by Horatio, Jr. Alger

Orphans, conduct of life, fathers and sons, and inheritance and succession, in Horatio, Jr. Alger’s Errand Boy; Or, How Phil Brent Won Success.

The Princess of Cleves

The Princess of Cleves

by Madame de (Marie-Madeleine Pioche de La Vergne) La Fayette

The Princess of Cleves was regarded by many as the beginning of the modern tradition of the psychological novel and a classic work. Its author is generally held to be Madame de La Fayette.

Manon Lescaut

Manon Lescaut

by abbé Prévost

Manon Lescaut tells a tragic love story about a nobleman (known only as the Chevalier des Grieux) and a common woman (Manon Lescaut). Their decision to live together without marriage is the start of a moral decline that also leads to gambling, fraud, theft, murder, and Manon's death as a deportee in New Orleans.

The Cost

The Cost

by David Graham Phillips

In The Cost, the film stars Violet Heming, Edwin Mordant, Jane Jennings, Ralph Kellard, Edward Arnold, and Clifford Grey. The movie was based on a 1904-novel by David Graham Phillips.

Little Lord Fauntleroy

Little Lord Fauntleroy

by Frances Hodgson Burnett

Little Lord Fauntleroy was published as a serial in St. Nicholas Magazine from November to October, then as a book by Scribner's (the publisher of St. Nicholas) on October 7, in New York. Little Lord Fauntleroy was also published that year in November by Frederick Warne & Co.

The Woodlanders

The Woodlanders

by Thomas Hardy

Love stories, Triangles, social classes, and forests and forestry, in Thomas Hardy’s Woodlanders.

Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm

Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm

by Kate Douglas Smith Wiggin

In Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, Published, it recounts Rebecca Rowena Randall and her aunts, one stern and one kind, in the fictional village of Riverboro, Maine. Rebecca's joy for life inspires her aunts, but she faces many trials in her young life, gaining wisdom and understanding.

The Shuttle

The Shuttle

by Frances Hodgson Burnett

In The Shuttle, one of Burnett's longer and more complicated books for adults, it takes up themes of intermarriages between wealthy American heiresses and impoverished British nobles.

Margret Howth: A Story of To-day

Margret Howth: A Story of To-day

by Rebecca Harding Davis

Rebecca Harding Davis wrote Margret Howth: A Story of To-day.

Heart of Darkness

Heart of Darkness

by Joseph Conrad

Heart of Darkness is widely regarded as a critique of European colonialism in Africa, whilst also examining the themes of power dynamics and morality. Although Conrad does not name the river on which most of the narrative takes place, at the time of writing, the Congo Free State—the location of the large and economically important Congo River—was a private colony of Belgium's King Leopold II.

The End of the Tether

The End of the Tether

by Joseph Conrad

In The End of the Tether, Published initially as accompaniment to 'Heart of Darkness' in a gathering of short stories titled 'Youth: A Narrative and Two Other Stories'. The three stories are: Youth - A Narrative; Heart of Darkness; and The End of The Tether.

Silas Marner

Silas Marner

by George Eliot

Silas Marner: The Weaver of Raveloe is the third novel by English author George Eliot; it was published on 2 April. A seemingly simple story of a linen weaver, Silas Marner is notable for its strong realist bent, as well as its sophisticated treatment of a variety of issues ranging from religion to industrialisation to community.

The Further Adventures of Robinson Crusoe

The Further Adventures of Robinson Crusoe

by Daniel Defoe

In The Further Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, just as in its significantly more popular predecessor, Robinson Crusoe, the first edition credits the work's fictional protagonist Robinson Crusoe as its author. The Further Adventures of Robinson Crusoe was published under the considerably longer original title: The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe; Being the Second and Last Part of His Life, And of the Strange Surprising Accounts of his Travels Round three Parts of the Globe.

The Mystery of Edwin Drood

The Mystery of Edwin Drood

by Charles Dickens

The Mystery of Edwin Drood was his final novel and was left unfinished when he died. Though the novel is named after the character Edwin Drood, it focuses more on Drood's uncle, John Jasper, a precentor, choirmaster and opium addict, who lusts after his pupil, Rosa Bud.

The Pickwick Papers

The Pickwick Papers

by Charles Dickens

The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club (also known as The Pickwick Papers) was the first novel by English author Charles Dickens, first published in serial form from March to November. Because of his success with Sketches by Boz published, Dickens was asked by the publisher Chapman & Hall to supply descriptions to explain a series of comic "cockney sporting plates" by illustrator Robert Seymour, and to connect them into a novel.

Master Humphrey's Clock

Master Humphrey's Clock

by Charles Dickens

Master Humphrey's Clock began with a frame story in which Master Humphrey tells about himself and his small circle of friends (which includes Mr. Pickwick), and their penchant for telling stories. Several short stories were included, followed by the novels The Old Curiosity Shop and Barnaby Rudge.

Vanity Fair

Vanity Fair

by William Makepeace Thackeray

Vanity Fair was published as a single volume in with the subtitle A Novel without a Hero. Vanity Fair is sometimes considered the "principal founder" of the Victorian domestic novel.

The Warden

The Warden

by Anthony Trollope

The Warden is the first book in the Chronicles of Barsetshire series, followed by Barchester Towers.

The Chimes A Goblin Story of Some Bells That Rang an Old Year out and a New Year In

The Chimes A Goblin Story of Some Bells That Rang an Old Year out and a New Year In

by Charles Dickens
